subjects.title: CCAF 5 - Context & Reliability
subjects.description: Domain 5 (15%) - lost in the middle, context budgeting, prompt caching, rate limits and retries, graceful degradation, and observability.

cards.question: Where should the most critical constraints go in a very long prompt?
cards.answer: Beginning and end. Attention is strongest at the edges of a long context, so critical content in the middle is the most likely to be under-weighted.

choices.text: At the beginning, and restated at the end
In the middle, surrounded by supporting context
Anywhere - position does not affect attention
Only at the very end, so it is freshest

hints: Where is attention strongest in a long context?

cards.question: Your agent's context fills up because a search tool returns full page bodies. What is the best fix?
cards.answer: Trim at the source: return titles, snippets, and ids, and add a separate fetch tool for the full body when it is actually needed. Compaction and bigger windows treat the symptom while the same flood recurs each call. `max_tokens` limits what Claude writes, not what tools return.

choices.text: Return snippets plus ids, with a separate fetch tool for the full text
Summarize the conversation after every tool call to reclaim the space
Switch to a model whose context window is large enough to hold the pages
Raise `max_tokens` so the long tool results fit in the response

hints: Fix it where the flood starts, not where it lands.

cards.question: When compacting a long agent conversation, which rule must you not break?
cards.answer: Never remove a `tool_use` without its matching `tool_result` (or vice versa). An orphaned pair makes the next request invalid.

choices.text: Never orphan a `tool_use` from its `tool_result` - remove complete pairs only
Never remove any message older than 10 turns
Always drop the system prompt first, since it is the largest block
Always summarize the most recent turns first

hints: There is one pair you must always remove together or keep together.

cards.question: 200,000 documents must be classified every night, with results needed by morning. Which approach fits?
cards.answer: Batch fits non-blocking, latency-tolerant work - overnight reports, weekly audits - at a 50% discount, with a processing window of up to 24 hours and no latency SLA. The batch discount also stacks with prompt caching. Note the trap: server tools such as web search can run inside a batch request, but your own tools cannot, because nothing can execute them and send results back mid-request.

choices.text: The Message Batches API, since the job is latency-tolerant and 50% cheaper
The synchronous API with high concurrency, so each document's latency stays predictable
The Message Batches API, running your own tools mid-request to enrich each document
The synchronous API on a smaller model, trading accuracy for a lower price

hints: Nobody is waiting at a screen. And one option asks batch to do something it cannot.

cards.question: Where should a key findings summary sit inside a long aggregated input?
cards.answer: Placing key findings summaries at the beginning and organizing detailed results with explicit section headers is the named mitigation for position effects. Models process the beginning and end reliably, and the middle is where findings get omitted.

choices.text: At the beginning, with detailed results organized under explicit section headers
At the end, so it is the last thing read before the model responds
In the middle, adjacent to the detailed results it is summarizing
Repeated at both ends, so its position cannot affect the outcome

hints: The middle is the one place it must not be.

cards.question: The customer is clearly angry, and their issue is a straightforward address change the agent can do. What is right?
cards.answer: Sentiment is an unreliable proxy for case complexity. The named skill is acknowledging frustration while offering resolution when the issue is within capability, escalating only if the customer reiterates the preference.

choices.text: Acknowledge the frustration, offer the fix, escalate only if they insist
Escalate immediately, since an angry customer is a retention risk for the business
Complete the address change first, then apologize for the inconvenience caused
Ask whether they would prefer a human before doing anything about the address

hints: The anger is real. The complexity is not.

cards.question: The return policy covers your own site's price drops. A customer wants a competitor's lower price matched. What should the agent do?
cards.answer: Escalation triggers include policy exceptions and gaps - not just complex cases. A policy that is silent or ambiguous on the specific request is a gap, and deciding it either way is the agent inventing policy.

choices.text: Escalate, because the policy is silent on this specific request
Decline, since the policy does not authorize matching a competitor's price
Approve it, treating a competitor price like an own-site price drop
Ask for the competitor's listing, then apply the standard price adjustment

hints: The policy does not say no. It does not say anything.

cards.question: A subagent's search times out. Which error report lets the coordinator recover intelligently?
cards.answer: Structured error context - failure type, what was attempted, partial results, alternatives - is what enables the coordinator to decide whether to retry with a modified query, try another approach, or proceed with a declared gap. Generic statuses hide exactly that.

choices.text: Failure type, the query attempted, partial results, and possible alternatives
A message stating that the search service is currently unavailable
The raw exception and stack trace from the underlying HTTP client
An empty result set flagged as successful, so synthesis can continue

hints: The coordinator has a decision to make. What does it need to make it?

cards.question: Two of six research areas had no available sources. How should the synthesis output handle that?
cards.answer: Structuring synthesis output with coverage annotations - well-supported versus gaps from unavailable sources - is the named skill. Silent omission produces a report that reads as complete, and filling gaps from general knowledge fabricates.

choices.text: Annotate coverage, marking which findings are well-supported and which areas have gaps
Omit those two areas entirely, so the report contains only supported findings
Include the two areas with the model's best general knowledge as a placeholder
Return an error, since a report covering four of six areas is incomplete

hints: The reader has to be able to see what is missing.

cards.question: How should a multi-agent exploration be designed to survive an interruption?
cards.answer: Designing crash recovery using structured agent state exports - manifests the coordinator loads on resume and injects into agent prompts - is the named skill. Holding everything in the coordinator's context means the crash takes all of it.

choices.text: Each agent exports state to a known location; the coordinator loads a manifest on resume
The coordinator keeps every subagent result in its own context until completion
Each agent writes a scratchpad file that the next agent reads at its own discretion
The session is resumed by name, since Claude Code persists conversation state itself

hints: There is a specific word for the file the coordinator reads on the way back.

cards.question: You automated the high-confidence extraction path. What keeps you informed about its error rate?
cards.answer: Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions is the named mechanism for ongoing error rate measurement and novel pattern detection. A fixed validation set only measures the failure modes it already contains.

choices.text: Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions, reviewed on an ongoing basis
The confidence scores themselves, monitored for any drop in their average value
Downstream complaints, which surface the errors that actually affect a consumer
A re-run of the labeled validation set on a fixed schedule every quarter

hints: You stopped looking at that bucket. Something has to keep looking.

cards.question: Field-level confidence scores come back from the model. What makes them usable for routing?
cards.answer: Field-level confidence scores are calibrated using labeled validation sets for routing review attention. Uncalibrated self-reported confidence is not a probability, so a threshold picked on the raw numbers means nothing.

choices.text: Calibrating the review routing thresholds against a labeled validation set
Averaging them per document, so one weak field does not divert it
Requiring the model to justify each score with its source text
Setting a round-number threshold and adjusting it when reviewers complain

hints: The number the model gives you is not yet a probability.

cards.question: Two credible sources give figures a year apart, and the report calls them contradictory. What was missing?
cards.answer: Requiring publication or data collection dates in structured outputs is what prevents temporal differences being misinterpreted as contradictions. A conflict annotation would have recorded the disagreement without explaining that there was none.

choices.text: Publication or data collection dates in the subagents' structured output
A conflict annotation, flagging the two values as inconsistent
A source reliability score, letting synthesis prefer one figure
A unit normalization step, since the figures may use different scales

hints: They do not disagree. They describe different moments.

cards.question: Extractions the model marks high-confidence are auto-approved and never reviewed. You need to know whether that population is drifting or developing new failure modes, without restoring full review. What should you implement?
cards.answer: Stratified random sampling of the auto-approved population is how its error rate stays measured and how new failure modes surface, without restoring full review. Reviewing what the downstream system rejected only sees failures that are already caught. Comparing value distributions signals that something changed without telling you whether it is wrong. A first-occurrence rule for new templates misses drift in familiar ones.

choices.text: Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions, reviewed on an ongoing basis.
A monthly review of every extraction the downstream system rejected as invalid.
A rule that any extraction from a new document template is reviewed on its first occurrence.
A comparison of this month's field value distributions against last month's as a drift alarm.

hints: You have to keep measuring a population you stopped looking at.

cards.question: Your extraction pipeline reports 97% field-level accuracy overall, and leadership wants to remove human review entirely. What is the necessary check before doing that?
cards.answer: An aggregate figure can hide a document type or a field that performs badly, so the accuracy has to be broken down by segment before the human is removed. A larger sample only sharpens the same aggregate. Three months of stability shows that a possibly misleading number is steady. A confidence threshold acts on scores that have not been validated per segment.

choices.text: Break the accuracy down by document type and by field to confirm no segment performs badly.
Increase the validation sample size until the overall accuracy estimate has a much tighter confidence interval.
Confirm the 97% figure is stable across the last three months before changing the process.
Set a model confidence threshold high enough that the remaining extractions are reliable.

hints: An average is a poor guide when the population is not uniform.
